ta-l1d44q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 44. Lombard excludes the error of those who limited God's power to the quality of things, asking whether it is limited to the goodness of things (refuting their reason that God cannot make better things than he does and destroying their position by argument) and to their mode (whether he can make what he makes in another or better way), and then answers a question that seemed to imply a diminution of divine power, whether God can always do what he once could. Four articles are announced: whether God could have made each thing better than he made it; whether he could have made the universe better; whether he could have made certain most excellent creatures better; and whether God can now do whatever he once could.
claims: God's power is not limited to the present goodness or mode of things.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e118.summary: First argument that God could not have made any creature better than it is. It belongs to the best to produce the best (Dionysius, Plato), and nothing can be better than the best.
claims: The best produces the best.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e121.summary: Second argument. Receiving from the Father is common to the Son and every creature (Basil), and the same argument holds of things of one concept, so as Augustine argues that God, without envy, could not beget a Son better than he begot, neither could he make creatures better than they are.
claims: The argument from no envy applies to creatures.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e124.summary: Third argument. An effect produced by a cause with its whole power cannot be made better by it, and God makes each creature with his whole power, his indivisible essence.
claims: God acts with his whole power.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e128.summary: Fourth argument. One thing falls short of another's goodness only by falling short of participating divine goodness, which is not from God, who relates equally to all (Dionysius), but from the thing's capacity.
claims: Inequality is from the capacity of things.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e131.summary: Sed contra. Addition is possible to any finite thing, and every creature's goodness is finite, and the omnipotent can do whatever can be done.
claims: The finite admits addition.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e134.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever nature does God can do, and nature improves things, as a man grows from childhood to youth.
claims: Nature improves things.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e137.summary: Thomas's determination. Each thing in itself has twofold goodness, as twofold being, since being and good are convertible: essential goodness (for a man, being living and rational) and accidental goodness (health, knowledge). God could have given each thing greater accidental goodness. As to essential goodness, he could have made another thing better than any created thing, but not made this thing of greater essential goodness, since adding to essential goodness would make not the same thing but another: as in numbers adding or subtracting a unit changes the species, so in definitions adding or subtracting a difference (Metaphysics 8), as adding 'rational' to the definition of ox makes not an ox but a man, and subtracting 'sensible' leaves only the life of trees. As God cannot make three, remaining three, have four units, though he can make a number greater than any, he cannot make this thing remain the same and have greater or lesser essential goodness, which would make affirmation and negation true together (Dist. 42).
claims: God can increase a thing's accidental goodness, and make better things, but cannot increase a thing's essential goodness while it remains the same.
Changing essential goodness changes the species, like adding to a number.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e140.summary: Reply to the first argument. Each thing in itself is not the best, except perhaps as attaining all its essential goodness, as three might be called greatest as attaining the quantity of its species; but in order to the universe it is best, as Augustine says.
claims: Each thing is best in relation to the universe.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e143.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though receiving from the Father is common to the Son and every creature by analogy, having it by nature is proper to him, so equality with the Father is owed him by nature, and if the Father had not begotten him equal when he could, he would be envious, withholding a dignity the Son should and could have. A creature can never reach God's equality, and no measure of goodness is owed it but by the determination of the divine will, so no envy follows if God could have made something better. So Hilary says God's will gave substance to all creatures, but nature gave it to the Son.
claims: Equality is owed to the Son by nature; creatures are owed only what God wills.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e147.summary: Reply to the third argument. Though God produces each creature with his whole infinite power, the quantity of goodness in the effect follows the maker's will, which commands the work that power executes.
claims: The effect's goodness follows God's will, not the measure of his power.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e150.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The diverse grades among beings come not only from things, whose capacities differ, but from the order of disposing wisdom, which assigns diverse capacities to things and then bestows its gifts by providence, participated differently according to the capacities God ordained.
claims: God's wisdom assigns the capacities themselves.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e153.summary: The other arguments are answered by the determination.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e165.summary: First argument that God could not have made the universe better. Augustine says the things God made are good singly and all together very good, and nothing can be better than the superlatively good.
claims: The universe is very good.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e168.summary: Second argument. The universe includes every good, and nothing can be better than every good.
claims: The universe includes all good.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e171.summary: Third argument. Better and good are found as things participate more divine perfections (Dionysius), and all communicable divine perfections have been communicated to some creatures.
claims: All communicable perfections are communicated.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e175.summary: Fourth argument. The more ordered, the better (Augustine defines evil as privation of order), and nothing in the universe is disordered, even evil being ordered by God.
claims: The universe is perfectly ordered.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e178.summary: Sed contra. The whiter is what is less mixed with black (the Philosopher), so the better is what is less mixed with evil, and God could have made a universe with no evil.
claims: A universe without evil would be better.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e181.summary: Second sed contra. Adding an equal to a greater makes the whole greater, so adding the better to the better makes the whole better, and an angel is better than a stone, so a universe all of angels would be much better, which God could make.
claims: A universe of angels would be better.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e184.summary: Thomas's determination. The good of the universe consists in a twofold order (Metaphysics 11): of its parts to one another and of the whole to its end, God, as an army has the order of its parts by their offices and the order to the leader's good, victory, the latter being chief and the reason for the former. The good of the parts' mutual order can be considered as to the parts ordered or as to their order. As to the parts, the universe could be better by adding more parts, creating many other species and filling more possible grades of goodness, since there is infinite distance between the highest creature and God, and so God could have made and can make a better universe, which would relate to this one as whole to part, neither wholly the same nor wholly different, an addition of goodness by discrete quantity; or intensively, all its parts improved, since improving some and not others would lessen the goodness of order, as in a lyre improving all strings gives sweeter harmony but improving only some gives dissonance. Improvement of all parts by accidental goodness could be done with the same parts and the same universe; by essential goodness it is possible to God, who can found infinitely many species, but then the parts and so the universe would not be the same. As to the order itself, it cannot be better by discrete quantity without adding parts, since nothing in the universe is disordered, but it could be better intensively with the same parts, as to the order following accidental goodness, since the more something redounds to a greater good the better its order; the order following essential goodness could be better only with other parts and another universe. The order to the end, on the side of the end, could not be better, since nothing can be better than God; as to the order itself, it could improve as the goodness and mutual order of the parts increased, being nearer to the end as they attained more likeness to divine goodness, the end of all.
claims: God could make a better universe by adding species or improving all parts, though with essential improvement it would be another universe.
The universe's order to its end cannot be better on the side of the end, God, but can as the parts grow in likeness to him.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e187.summary: Reply to the first argument. Augustine speaks of the universe's order given the same nature of its parts, and so the order could not be better.
claims: Given these parts, the order is the best.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e190.summary: Reply to the second argument. We speak not of 'universe' as a name but of this thing now called the universe, which, though containing every actual good, does not contain every good God can make.
claims: The universe contains all actual good, not all possible good.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e194.summary: Reply to the third argument. There are many modes of participating the same divine perfection, as divine wisdom is participated one way in intellectual substances, another in rational ones, humans, and down to brutes with sensitive cognition; so though all perhaps communicable perfections have been communicated, not in every mode in which creatures could participate them.
claims: Perfections can be participated in more modes than realized.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e197.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Though the universe's order cannot be better by more of its parts being ordered, it could be better if ordered to a better good as proximate end, which would happen if better parts were made.
claims: Better parts would make a better order.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e200.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. A universe with no evil would not have as much goodness as this one, since it would not have as many good natures as this, where some good natures have no evil joined and some do, and it is better that both natures exist than only one.
claims: A universe with fallible natures is better than one without.
concepts: evil and the good of the universe

ta-l1d44q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the second sed contra. Though an angel is absolutely better than a stone, both natures together are better than one only, so a universe with angels and other things is better than one of angels alone, since the universe's perfection consists essentially in the diversity of natures filling the various grades of goodness, not in multiplying individuals of one nature.
claims: The universe's perfection lies in diversity of natures, not multiplication of the best.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e215.summary: First argument that God could not make Christ's humanity better. The nearer to God the better, and nothing created can be nearer God than what is united to him in unity of person.
claims: Hypostatic union is the closest possible.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e218.summary: Second argument. Nothing can be greater than the infinite, and the goodness of Christ's soul is infinite, since the Spirit was given him without measure (John 3).
claims: Christ's grace is infinite.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e221.summary: Third argument that nothing better than the Blessed Virgin is possible. Anselm says it was fitting that the Virgin God prepared as mother for his only Son should shine with a purity greater than which none under God can be conceived, and God cannot make anything equal to himself.
claims: Mary's purity is the greatest under God.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e225.summary: Fourth argument. The angel was made near God (Augustine), and the Virgin is exalted above the choirs of angels (Jerome, the Church's chant), so nothing can be nearer God or better.
claims: Mary is above the angels.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e228.summary: Fifth argument that nothing is better than created beatitude, which is the state perfect by the aggregation of all goods (Boethius), and nothing is better than all good.
claims: Beatitude contains all goods.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e231.summary: Sed contra. The uncreated good exceeds every created good infinitely, and there can be many intermediates between the infinitely distant, so God can make many things better than any created good.
claims: Infinite distance allows intermediates.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e234.summary: Thomas's determination. As anything better than any created good is possible, since it is finite, nothing can be better than the uncreated good, since it is infinite. A creature's goodness can be considered absolutely, and then something better than any creature is possible; or in comparison to the uncreated good, and then the creature's dignity receives a kind of infinity from the infinite it is compared to: human nature as united to God, the Blessed Virgin as Mother of God, grace as joining to God, the universe as ordered to God. Among these comparisons there is a twofold order. First, the nobler the relation to God, the nobler the thing, so human nature in Christ is noblest, related to God by union, then the Virgin, from whose womb the flesh united to divinity was taken, and so on. Second, some comparisons are by relation only, like the universe to its end and the mother to the son, so from their dignity no absolute judgement follows, that nothing could be better than the Virgin, but only a relative one, that none could be mother of a better son, or a universe ordered to a greater good. The comparison by union is also by being, so the absolute judgement of the united nature follows the goodness of the comparison: nothing can be better than Christ as man; a judgement apart from that comparison is only relative, that human nature in Christ, as created, could be bettered, since nature considered apart from its being is only by a conception of reason.
claims: Creatures related to the infinite good receive a relative infinity of dignity: Christ's humanity, the Mother of God, grace, the ordered universe.
Christ as man cannot be bettered, since union is by being; Mary's dignity as Mother cannot be exceeded relationally, though absolutely a better creature is possible.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e237.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though human nature is united to divinity in person, the natures remain infinitely distant, and from that side something better than the human nature in Christ is possible, not from the side by which it is united.
claims: The united natures remain infinitely distant.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e240.summary: Reply to the second argument. The habitual grace infused in Christ's soul is not simply and per se infinite but in some respect, as the power of an intelligence is infinite downward (Dist. 43): Christ's grace is infinite in some respect as able to produce all effects of grace, and incidentally as concurring in the union with the infinite good as a medium of congruity and in Christ's operation, which has infinite value as the operation of a divine person.
claims: Christ's habitual grace is infinite only in some respect.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e244.summary: Reply to the third argument. Purity increases by withdrawal from its contrary, so some creature can be found than which nothing purer can be among creatures, if stained by no contagion of sin, and such was the Virgin's purity, immune from original and actual sin. Yet she was under God, since there was in her the potency to sin. Goodness increases by approach to a term infinitely distant, the supreme good, so something better than any finite good is possible.
claims: Mary's purity is unsurpassable among creatures, being free of original and actual sin; goodness, by contrast, can always increase.
She remained under God by having the potency to sin.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e247.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Between angels and God there is infinite distance, so God could make many intermediate grades, and though the Virgin is exalted above the angels, not to God's equality, so infinite distance remains and something better is still possible.
claims: Infinite distance remains above Mary.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e250.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Created beatitude has a kind of infinity from joining to the infinite good, since in itself it comprises all goods participable by man, so if nature's capacity were greater, participation and beatitude would be more perfect, as one saint's beatitude exceeds another's. Boethius means this definition fits uncreated beatitude essentially and others by participation.
claims: Created beatitude could be greater with greater capacity.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e263.summary: First argument that God cannot do everything he once could. His power extends to individuals as well as species, making matter and form, and before Socrates existed he could make Socrates, so with Socrates existing he could make him, which is false, since a thing's substance would exist twice.
claims: God cannot make an existing thing again.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e266.summary: Second argument. Once God could not become incarnate, but now he cannot not have become incarnate, as no past can not have been.
claims: The Incarnation cannot be undone.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e269.summary: Third argument, against 'as he could once do it, he can now have done it, one and the same ability'. Likewise one blinded can now have seen, having once been able to see, yet we do not say he can do whatever he could.
claims: The blind man parallel.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e273.summary: Fourth argument. From eternity God could not predestine Peter, whom he freely predestined, but now he cannot not predestine him, since one cannot be first predestined and then not.
claims: Predestination cannot be revoked.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e276.summary: Sed contra. The quantity of power follows the number of objects, and God's power cannot diminish.
claims: Divine power cannot diminish.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e279.summary: Thomas's determination. Someone is denied ability either by defect of power, as one without sight cannot see, or because the object lacks the character of possible, as one with sight cannot see a sound. In the first way God is unable to do nothing, his power being most perfect; in the second he is said unable to do some things, like making the same be and not be at once, which would better be called unable to be done than God unable to do them. Likewise someone cannot do what he could either by losing a power he had, which does not fit God, and Lombard's solution proceeds this way, or by change in the object, which loses the character of possible it had, since active power regards something operable, and when something is already determined as present in act or has passed into the past it loses the character of possible, and God is said unable to do it, though it is the same thing signified by different enunciations by the difference of times.
claims: God's power never diminishes; things cease to be possible objects once present or past.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e282.summary: Reply to the first argument. When a thing already exists in act, it loses the character of possible to be made.
claims: Existing things are no longer makeable.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e285.summary: Likewise to the second argument, which concerned the past.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e288.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Someone can have done this' can mean the past belongs to the possible, which is nothing, since the past loses the character of possible; or it concerns the going out of the possible from the power, and so God can have done this because he has the power by which he did it. This does not fit the blind man, who lacks the power by which he once saw, so it is in no way true that he can have seen.
claims: God can have done what he did, having the same power; the blind man lacks it.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e292.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The act of predestination is measured by eternity and does not pass into the past, so it always has the character of possible in the same way, as from the liberality of the divine will; on the side of its effect it passes into the past and so loses the character of possible.
claims: Predestination's act remains free; its effects become past.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e295.summary: The fifth, the sed contra, is answered by the determination.

ta-l1d44q1-d1e304.summary: An expositio textus. 'Though he cannot now become incarnate' seems false, since as the Son assumed flesh the Father could and can (III, Dist. 1), so it seems he could become incarnate now. Lombard means the numerically same incarnation that once occurred; if he became incarnate now, it would not be the same incarnation numerically but another.
claims: Lombard means the numerically same incarnation.

ta-l1d44q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 44 divides Lombard's refutation of those who limited God's power to the quality and mode of things, and announces four articles on making things, the universe, and excellent creatures better, and on whether God can do all he once could.
claims: God's power is not limited to things as they are.

ta-l1d44q1-Dd1e110.summary: Article 1 holds that God can increase a thing's accidental goodness and make better things, but not increase a thing's essential goodness while it remains the same, since that would change its species, like adding a unit to a number. Each thing is best in relation to the universe, no envy follows since creatures are owed only what God wills, the effect's goodness follows God's will, and his wisdom assigns things' capacities.
claims: God cannot better a thing essentially while it remains itself, but can make better things.

ta-l1d44q1-Dd1e157.summary: Article 2 holds that God could make a better universe, by adding species or improving all its parts, though essential improvement would make another universe. Given these parts, its order is best, and its order to its end cannot be better on God's side. A universe with fallible natures is better than one without, and its perfection lies in diversity of natures, not in multiplying the best.
claims: God could make a better universe; this one is best given its parts.
The universe's perfection lies in diversity of grades.

ta-l1d44q1-Dd1e207.summary: Article 3 holds that creatures related to the infinite good receive a relative infinity of dignity. Christ as man cannot be bettered, since union is by being, though his humanity as created could be. Mary's dignity as Mother of God cannot be exceeded relationally, and her purity, free of original and actual sin, is unsurpassable among creatures, though a better creature is absolutely possible. Christ's grace is infinite only in some respect, and created beatitude could be greater.
claims: Christ's humanity, the Mother of God, grace, and the universe have relative infinite dignity.
Mary was free of original and actual sin.

ta-l1d44q1-Dd1e255.summary: Article 4 holds that God's power never diminishes; things cease to be possible objects once present or past, so God cannot make what exists or undo the past. He can have done what he did, having the same power, unlike the blind man, and the act of predestination remains free in eternity while its effects become past.
claims: God can do all he could; only objects change in possibility.

ta-l1d44q1-Dd1e299.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 44 explains that God cannot now become incarnate in the numerically same incarnation, though another incarnation would be possible.
claims: A new incarnation would be numerically different.

ta-l1d44q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 44 asks whether God could make things better. Article 1 holds that he could improve things accidentally and make better things, but not improve a thing essentially while it remains itself. Article 2 holds that he could make a better universe, though this one is best given its parts, its perfection lying in diversity of natures. Article 3 holds that Christ's humanity, the Mother of God, grace, and the universe have relative infinite dignity from their relation to God. Mary's purity was unsurpassable, free of original and actual sin. Article 4 holds that God's power never diminishes, though past and present things cease to be possible.
claims: God could make better things and a better universe, but not improve a thing essentially while it remains itself.
Christ's humanity cannot be bettered; Mary's purity is unsurpassable among creatures.
God's power never diminishes.
